newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Chirac honours veterans of Hungary's 1956 uprising.
newsitem.headline: Chirac honours veterans of Hungary's 1956 uprising.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, on a two-day state visit, paid tribute on Thursday to Hungary's failed 1956 revolution when he awarded medals to President Arpad Goncz and 12 other veterans of the uprising.
The decorations came on the day Hungary's Supreme Court made its first convictions of those who helped put down the revolution four decades ago.

"I wish to pay homage, in the name of all French and Europeans who followed your insurrection with passionate attention and impotent anger, to your courage and to your commitment," Chirac said at the award ceremony.
Several thousands Hungarians were killed in fighting when Soviet troops invaded Hungary in November 1956 to crush an uprising against the Hungarian Stalinist regime of Matyas Rakosi.

Around 300 were later executed and hundreds more imprisoned, including Goncz himself, who spent six years in jail, and to whom Chirac gave France's highest award La Grand Croix de la Legion d'Honneur.
"For us to receive these decorations we needed to stay alive and in order to stay alive others had to give their lives," Goncz said.

Others decorated included Miklos Vasarhelyi, secretary to the revolution's leader Imre Nagy and Margit Nemeth, a secretary at the French Embassy from 1946 to 1950 who was imprisoned for six years for refusing to spy for Hungary.

Chirac's awards coincided with a Hungarian Supreme Court ruling on Thursday that three men were guilty of committing crimes against humanity when they fired on demonstrators in December 1956 in Salgotarjan, in northern Hungary, killing 47.

The sentencing of the men to two years in prison marked the first time the prosecution managed to bring convictions to their final judicial stage in the drawn-out struggle to put totalitarianism's henchmen behind bars.

Addressing a gathering at Budapest's parliament soon after his arrival Chirac set the year 2000 as a target date for Hungary's accession to the European Union, saying it was a question of "political will".
"I want your country to join the European Union in the year 2000 -- France will do everything to ensure that date is respected," he said.
EU experts have said that deadline is unrealistic and it will probably take at least two years longer for the first former communist Central European states to join.
To warm applause, Chirac said such a target date was achievable if everyone "made the necessary efforts".
"Certain people say 'it's too soon, we won't make it' -- that is to forget the years you have waited," he said. "It is also to forget that a timetable is above all a question of political will."
The French president also expressed his "unqualified support" for Hungary's application to join NATO, which he described as a historic opportunity to "bring together the European family".

Chirac's visit to Hungary is the first by a French head of state since the end of communism. His predecessor Francois Mitterrand visited Budapest just months before Hungary held its first democratic elections in 1990.
